haiku-low.q1: The document is removed. An archived row, like a draft row or a delete, removes the search document. Only active rows may appear in search.
haiku-low.q2: The index returns a version conflict. The older write is counted as stale, not treated as an error, and the newer version stays.
haiku-low.q3: It retries the same batch, waiting 1 s and doubling up to 60 s. The offset is not committed, and it never skips ahead until accepted.
haiku-low.q4: It is written to catalog.products.dlq with the error. An alert is raised, and the indexer carries on with the next changes.
haiku-low.q5: WAL piles up. An alert fires at 20 GB, and at 50 GB ops drop the slot. After that, only a full rebuild restores search.
haiku-low.q6: The alias products moves atomically to products_v4, but only when it is under 5 s behind and its count is within 0.5% of active rows.
haiku-low.q7: Progress is stored as Kafka offsets for the indexer's consumer group. An offset is committed only after the index acknowledges every write up to it.
haiku-low.q8: It restarts from the last committed offset and re-reads uncommitted events. Re-applying them is safe because the version rule keeps the newest version.
haiku-low.q9: A catch-up consumer with its own offsets reads catalog.products and writes into products_v4 using the same rules as the live path.
haiku-low.q11: The live indexer keeps writing products_v3 for 48 hours after the switch, so the alias can move back. No step says how this ends or removes it.
haiku-low.q12: The alias is never moved, so search keeps querying products_v3, which the live indexer keeps writing. Whether catch-up resumes or restarts is not decided.

sonnet.q1: The document is removed from the index (a draft or archived row removes the document; only active rows may appear in search).
sonnet.q2: The write is rejected with a version conflict because its commit_lsn is lower. It is counted as stale, not treated as an error, and the newer version stays.
sonnet.q3: It retries the same batch with backoff: 1 s, doubling, capped at 60 s. It does not commit the offset and never skips ahead. It retries until accepted.
sonnet.q4: It is written to the DLQ topic catalog.products.dlq with the error, an alert is raised, and the indexer carries on. A person fixes it later. (Whether the offset moves before or after the DLQ write is acknowledged is an open question; the draft assumes after.)
sonnet.q5: Postgres keeps WAL for search_slot, with an alert at 20 GB. At 50 GB ops drop the slot to protect the primary. After that, only a full rebuild restores search.
sonnet.q6: The search API always queries the alias products. One atomic alias move points it at the new index (products_v4). Before the move, the new index must be under 5 s behind and its document count within 0.5% of the active row count.
sonnet.q7: In Kafka, as consumer offsets stored for the indexer's consumer group. The offset is committed only after the index has acknowledged every write up to that point.
sonnet.q8: It restarts from the last committed offset and re-reads the uncommitted events. Re-applying them is safe because the version rule keeps the newest version.
sonnet.q9: A catch-up consumer reads catalog.products with its own offsets and writes into the new index with the same rules as the live path. The rebuild job records the Kafka position when it starts. Exactly where the catch-up starts is an open question; it must start at or before the snapshot's point, and the 7-day retention limits how far back it can go.
sonnet.q10: NOT STATED. The snapshot rows have no commit_lsn, and the plan has not decided what version they carry. The snapshot's LSN is one option.
sonnet.q11: products_v3 is kept for 48 hours and the live indexer keeps writing to it, so moving the alias back loses no change made after the switch. After 48 hours the rollback window ends. No step removes products_v3, and how the dual writes work is undecided.
sonnet.q12: Search is not affected. The alias is never moved until the new index is ready, so search keeps using products_v3, and the live indexer keeps writing to it. The plan does not say whether a failed backfill resumes or restarts. If the catch-up falls more than 7 days behind, the rebuild must start again.
